a1.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley states that LeadIQ, its AI-powered lead distribution platform, focuses on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with its financial advisors.
items.quote: LeadIQ, our AI-powered lead distribution platform, focusing on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with our financial advisors.
items.definition: our AI-powered lead distribution platform

items.text: Morgan Stanley states that LeadIQ uses AI to help introduce its advisors to clients who are interested in advice, as technology used on the revenue side.
items.quote: LeadIQ, for example, which is helping us introduce our advisors to our clients who are interested in advice, that's happening using AI.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states it is making ongoing investments in its world-class platform, including investments to support its advisors, a build-out of E*TRADE capabilities, and the expansion of its workplace channel.
items.quote: Ongoing investments in our world-class platform, including investments to support our advisors, a build-out of E*TRADE capabilities, and the expansion of our essential workplace channel, serve as an engine for future growth.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states it is using its scale to invest in broadening capabilities for financial advisors that are difficult for others to replicate, including alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states its growth plans embed the increasing adoption of AI tools throughout the enterprise and inside its client base.
items.quote: Our growth plans embed the increasing adoption of AI tools throughout the enterprise and inside our client base.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states it has been giving tools to its advisors to attract new clients and existing clients and assets held away.
items.quote: we're also bringing in new clients, and that's a lot of the tools that we've been giving to our advisors.

items.text: Morgan Stanley references 'next best action' tools through which advisors send next best actions to their individual retail clients.
items.quote: Remember all the stuff we used to talk about with next best action, etc., where advisors were sending next best actions to their individual retail clients.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states it continues to invest, deepening competitive moats in areas like its expanded collaboration with Carta in private markets and in digital assets through announced partnerships with Zero Hash.
items.quote: we continue to invest, deepening our competitive moats in areas like our expanded collaboration with Carta in private markets and in digital assets through announced partnerships with Zero Hash.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states its scale supports continued investment in future technology, including AI and digital tools.
items.quote: our scale supports continued investment in future technology, including AI and digital tools.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states that its technology enables it to be a differentiator in its favor across the advisor-led and integrated wealth funnel, making technology a competitive advantage for its advisors.
items.quote: we have built a number of advantages that not only allow us to preserve our moat, but actually make technology a differentiator in our favor.

a4.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley management says the firm continues to invest in Wealth, Institutional Securities and Investment Management via human capital and technology, with growth plans embedding the increasing adoption of AI tools throughout the enterprise and inside its client base.
items.quote: We continue to invest in each of our three business segments: Wealth, Institutional Securities, and Investment Management via human capital and technology. Our growth plans embed the increasing adoption of AI tools throughout the enterprise and inside our client base.

items.text: Management states the firm is using its scale to invest in broadening capabilities for financial advisors that are difficult for others to replicate, including alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

items.text: Management describes early AI use cases including LeadIQ, an AI-powered lead distribution platform focused on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with the firm's financial advisors.
items.quote: These include the DevGen AI tool, which enhances developer efficiency by modernizing code, Parable, an interactive tool that quickly analyzes and summarizes data, and LeadIQ, our AI-powered lead distribution platform, focusing on matching workplace and self-directed relationships and facilitating engagement with our financial advisors.

items.text: Management describes technology priorities for the advisor business as including protecting client assets and resiliency, and notes that world-class technology can help financial advisors by doing a lot of the early work for client decisions.
items.quote: Third, and this is critical, is the ability to protect client assets... if the technology is world-class, folks want to make decisions with their financial advisers based on the complexity and singularity of their own financial needs... that is something that technology can help do a lot of the early work.

items.text: Management describes using technology for both efficiency (cost side) and revenue (including some AI), as part of the investment story in technology, including in the E*TRADE franchise and E*TRADE Pro.
items.quote: We are also using technology to help us from an efficiency perspective, both on the cost and the revenue side. I'd note to you that some of the AI that we've been doing is actually also on the revenue side.

items.text: Management describes that against its platform of self-directed, workplace and advisor-led channels, the firm has built advantages that make technology a differentiator in its favor.
items.quote: And against that platform, we have built a number of advantages that not only allow us to preserve our moat, but actually make technology a differentiator in our favor.

items.text: Management states the firm's scale supports continued investment in future technology, including AI and digital tools, positioning it to lead as the future of wealth management takes shape.
items.quote: while our scale supports continued investment in future technology, including AI and digital tools. Together, these strengths provide us with a powerful competitive advantage that positions us to lead as the future of wealth management takes shape.

items.text: Management describes the firm as having been overweighted to AI from the early days in wealth, citing work done with OpenAI.
items.quote: We were, as you know, overweighted to AI from the early days in wealth with some of the work we did with OpenAI.

items.text: Management describes LeadIQ as using AI to introduce the firm's advisors to clients who are interested in advice, using technology on both the revenue and expense side to drive margin.
items.quote: So LeadIQ, for example, which is helping us introduce our advisors to our clients who are interested in advice, that's happening using AI. So there's technology that can be used both on the revenue side and on the expense side.

items.text: Management describes investing in all processes and systems to build robust infrastructure, across the technology side, better understanding of data, and better servicing of clients.
items.quote: we've been investing in all of our processes and our systems in order to engage and make sure that we have a robust infrastructure... that has to do with everything that I mentioned across the technology side, across better understanding our data, better servicing our clients.

items.text: Morgan Stanley's strategic update deck describes a market-leading platform to power growth for financial advisors.
items.quote: Market Leading Platform to Power Growth for Financial Advisors

a4.MS.reason: Multiple passages contain management's descriptions of technology priorities for the advisor (Wealth Management) business, including AI adoption, advisor capability investments, efficiency and revenue technology, and AI-powered tools like LeadIQ.

claims.text: On this evidence, the comparison can be made, and Merrill is the most explicit of the five: in its Wealth Continuum, Bank of America/Merrill explicitly names 'Mass Affluent' as a client segment, defined as clients with $500K to $1MM in assets, alongside 'High Net Worth' ($1MM–$10MM) (BAC-DECK-2025-investor-day#12). By contrast, Morgan Stanley names 'individual investors' and 'high and ultra-high net worth individuals' but never uses the term 'mass-affluent' (MS-10K-2025#125, MS-10K-2025#419); Schwab names 'affluent' clients and wealth tiers spanning 'new investors to ultra high net worth' rather than 'mass-affluent' (SCHW-TR-2025Q4#11, SCHW-TR-2026Q3#11, SCHW-DECK-2026Q3#23); and Edward Jones names 'individual investors,' 'High Net Worth,' and 'Next Generation investors' but not 'mass-affluent' (EDJ-10K-2025#9, EDJ-10K-2025#88). Raymond James does not name a mass-affluent segment in the documents searched. The comparison is valid for naming explicitness: Merrill explicitly names the segment, while the others name broader or different (higher-wealth or younger) categories.

first.label: not_found

first.label: not_found
first.reason: None of the passages state what communication and engagement channels younger investors prefer; the only related mentions are Edward Jones's own initiatives (a digital platform for Next Generation investors) and general statements about changing demographics and digital experiences, not a statement of younger investors' preferred channels.

a3.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones states that one of its new-client initiatives is "a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors," indicating the firm is targeting younger investors through a digital service model rather than its traditional full-service branch model.
items.quote: a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors

items.text: Edward Jones states its continued ability to compete may be adversely impacted by "generational wealth transfer, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values," pointing to evolving preferences among younger/demographically shifting clients toward technology and expanded offerings.
items.quote: generational wealth transfer, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values

a3.EDJ.reason: The passages give partial, firm-framed evidence about younger (Next Generation) investors' orientation toward digital platforms and technology, but do not explicitly state a self-directed versus full-service preference.

a4.EDJ.label: not_found

first.label: not_found

a5.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones states it is pursuing a new digital platform initiative, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors, as one of several initiatives to meet clients' planning, investing, saving, spending, borrowing and comprehensive needs.
items.quote: These initiatives also include targeting new clients: High Net Worth, focused on attracting and serving high net worth clients through expanded advice, planning, products and services across multiple service models; Workplace, which connects local business owners and their employees with financial solutions through their workplace; and a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.

items.text: Edward Jones announced it has taken a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken, with the stated intention of integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities more directly into Edward Jones to support its value proposition and advisor conversations with clients, though the firm notes it is still determining its actual deployment strategy.
items.quote: Edward Jones announced that they have taken a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken, with an explicit intention that the investment is a step towards integrating Quicken's personal financial management capabilities more directly into Edward Jones as a way to support their value proposition and advisor conversations with clients.

a5.EDJ.reason: The passages state current/recent digital initiatives, including a digital platform explicitly aimed at Next Generation investors and a technology investment to enhance digital personal financial management, which bear on alignment with younger investors' preferences.

a6.EDJ.label: fact

items.text: Edward Jones states that its initiatives to meet clients' planning, investing, saving, spending, borrowing and comprehensive needs include targeting new clients, including a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.
items.quote: These initiatives also include targeting new clients: High Net Worth, focused on attracting and serving high net worth clients through expanded advice, planning, products and services across multiple service models; Workplace, which connects local business owners and their employees with financial solutions through their workplace; and a new digital platform, focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors.

items.text: Edward Jones states its strategic ambition includes anticipating clients' needs with the right offering at the right time, now and for generations to come, and attracting and serving new client segments.
items.quote:
Anticipate clients' needs with the right offering at the right time, now and for generations to come

• Attract and serve new client segments

items.text: Edward Jones states its continued ability to compete and adapt its business model may be adversely impacted by generational wealth transfer and changing client demographics, preferences and values, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs.
items.quote: The Partnership's continued ability to compete and adapt its business model may be adversely impacted by the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values.

items.text: Edward Jones states it addresses strategic risks, most notably competition for clients and personnel in light of the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, and changing client demographics, preferences and values, through initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact.
items.quote: The Partnership seeks to address its strategic risks, most notably competition for clients and personnel in light of the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, changing client demographics, preferences and values, technology, artificial intelligence, and regulatory changes, through its initiatives to deliver enhanced value and impact for millions of current and potential clients, colleagues and communities.

a6.EDJ.reason: The passages state Edward Jones's strategy and priorities relevant to younger/next-generation and new client segments, including a digital platform for Next Generation investors and attention to generational wealth transfer and changing demographics.

items.text: Younger investors learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and Schwab meets them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.

claims.text: The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (October 2025), management said younger investors learn about finances primarily through social media and family, and that Schwab is meeting them in the channels where they turn for information about investing.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (October 2025), management said younger investors' top online resource for learning about finances is YouTube, and that Schwab is 'the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers.'
The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 2Q25 earnings call (July 2025), management said young investors want to think about how to pay off their college debt and how to buy a house.

The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (October 2025), management said younger traders turn to Schwab because they recognize the potential of trading to help build wealth over time, and for the platforms, tools, education, coaching, expertise, and service Schwab provides.
The Charles Schwab Corporation: On the 3Q25 earnings call (October 2025), the CEO said crypto 'will certainly appeal to young investors.'

Industry research: A Bank of America Private Bank study (published June 2026) reports that younger investors (Gen Z and Millennials, ages 21 to 45) are reshaping how wealth is built and diversified, embracing alternative investments and emerging technologies.
Industry research: The same study reports that 67% of younger investors (ages 21 to 45) believe traditional stocks and bonds can no longer deliver above-average returns.

Industry research: The study reports that younger investors allocate nearly half as much to stocks as older generations, while allocating more to alternatives (15%) and crypto (13%) than older investors.

Industry research: The study reports that crypto ranks as the #1 wealth-creation opportunity for young wealthy investors: 29% rank it #1, 58% currently own crypto (up from 49% in 2024), and 92% either own or are interested.
Industry research: The study reports that 88% of younger investors say they are likely to allocate more to alternatives in the next few years, compared with just 15% of Boomers and Silents.

Industry research: FINRA investor research (published December 2025) reports that younger investors (under 35) are much more likely to own individual stocks than mutual funds (82 percent vs. 47 percent).

Industry research: FINRA investor research (published December 2025) reports that younger investors (ages 18-34) are much more likely than older investors to have an options trading account (68%) and to have traded options (43%).

Industry research: FINRA investor research (published December 2025) reports that younger respondents are much more likely than older respondents to invest for reasons other than long-term profits; half or more of those under 35 say they invest for social responsibility, entertainment, and social activity reasons.

Industry research: FINRA investor research (published December 2025) reports that among those who have purchased meme stocks or other viral investments, 66% cite entertainment and 65% social activity as reasons for investing.

Industry research: A Bank of America Private Bank study (published June 2024) reports that younger investors (ages 21 to 43) believe it is no longer possible to achieve above-average investment returns by investing solely in traditional stocks and bonds, a view held by a much smaller share of investors over age 44.

Industry research: The same study reports that among younger high-net-worth investors (ages 21 to 43), 47% of portfolios are in stocks and bonds (vs 74% for over-44), 17% is allocated to alternatives, 93% plan to allocate more to alternatives, and 49% own cryptocurrencies.

Comparison: Edward Jones's younger-investor disclosures are forward-looking and initiative-based—a new digital platform targeting Next Generation investors, an acknowledgment of generational wealth transfer as a strategic risk, and a minority stake in Quicken—whereas Schwab discloses detailed quantitative metrics on younger-client acquisition (for example, approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households being Gen Z and millennials as of 3Q26) and names specific younger-investor offerings (Schwab Starter Kit, Schwab Teen Investor Account, no/low commissions, YouTube, crypto). Merrill's and Raymond James's cited materials concern next-generation financial advisors (recognition lists and a next-gen advisor recruiting strategy) rather than younger investors or clients, and Morgan Stanley's disclosures were not found; the quantitative metrics are therefore not comparable across firms (different definitions and scopes), so the comparison can be made only qualitatively at the level of disclosures and initiatives.

a3.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's integrated-firm client journey includes 'Founders Wealth Strategies' capabilities and, under 'Preserve Wealth,' 'Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation' and 'Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning,' indicating the firm retains wealth across generations through family office, trust and estate planning services.
items.quote: Founders Wealth Strategies ... Preserve Wealth ... Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation ... Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning

items.text: Morgan Stanley is investing to broaden capabilities for its financial advisors that include 'family office and OCIO,' alongside alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets and tailored lending, which support retaining multi-generational wealth.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

a3.MS.reason: The passages describe the firm's family office, trust & estate planning, and founders wealth strategies as capabilities used to preserve and retain wealth, which directly addresses preparing for wealth passing to heirs.

a4.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management had 15,950 Wealth Management representatives (financial advisors) as of December 31, 2020.
items.quote: Wealth Management representatives 15,950 15,469 15,468 3% 3%

items.text: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management had 15,469 Wealth Management representatives as of September 30, 2020.
items.quote: Wealth Management representatives 15,950 15,469 15,468 3% 3%

items.text: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management had 15,468 Wealth Management representatives as of December 31, 2019.
items.quote: Wealth Management representatives 15,950 15,469 15,468 3% 3%

items.text: Morgan Stanley for years has deferred a small amount of each advisor's gross revenue as 'deferred compensation' and required advisors to stay at the firm for years in order to vest, a retention mechanism known as 'golden handcuffs'.
items.quote: Giants like Morgan Stanley for years have taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue, called it deferred compensation, and required advisors to stay for years in order to vest.

items.text: Morgan Stanley is not introducing retention bonuses as part of its 2027 pay plan for advisors, but is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, so advisors must generate that much more revenue to receive the same pay.
items.quote: Morgan Stanley is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors have to generate that much more revenue to see the same pay next year.

items.text: Morgan Stanley will increase the cash component of its advisor compensation as it transitions deferred compensation plan (DCP) economic hedges to derivative instruments, changes it says support its overall investment into its financial advisors and simplify its compensation program.
items.quote: we will also increase the cash component of our advisor compensation... these changes support our overall investment into our financial advisors and will help simplify our compensation program.

items.text: Morgan Stanley states its ability to retain and attract qualified employees is critical to its success, and that failure to attract, integrate, and retain highly qualified employees or successfully transition key roles may materially adversely affect its performance.
items.quote: If we are unable to continue to attract, integrate and retain highly qualified employees or successfully transition key roles, or do so at levels or in forms necessary to maintain our competitive position, our performance, including our competitive position and results of operations, could be materially adversely affected.

items.text: Morgan Stanley notes advisor-led flows were particularly strong, originating from new advisors attracted to the strength of the workplace channel.
items.quote: Advisor-led flows were particularly strong, originating from new advisors who are attracted to the strength of the workplace, as well as assets that originated from workplace.

a4.MS.reason: Passages state Morgan Stanley's advisor headcount figures (2020 supplement) and its advisor retention/compensation/succession-related measures, which directly address how it manages its advisor force.

a5.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's strategic update deck shows the firm serves founders and employees across their growth cycle (from early stage through public company) with offerings including Founders Wealth Strategies, Private Shares Trading & Lending, IPO Execution and Support Services, Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits, Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation, Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning, and Unlock Liquidity.
items.quote: Corporates / Founders / Employees / Early Stage / Public Company / Invest for the Future / Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits / Founders Wealth Strategies / Preserve Wealth / Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation / Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning / Unlock Liquidity / Private Shares Trading & Lending / IPO Execution and Support Services / Optimize for Growth

items.text: Morgan Stanley states it is using scale to invest in broadening capabilities for financial advisors, including alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

items.text: Morgan Stanley reports it continues to invest to deepen competitive moats, including an expanded collaboration with Carta in private markets and in digital assets through announced partnerships with Zero Hash.
items.quote: we continue to invest, deepening our competitive moats in areas like our expanded collaboration with Carta in private markets and in digital assets through announced partnerships with Zero Hash.

items.text: Morgan Stanley identifies strategic initiatives such as its acquisition of EquityZen, expanded partnership with Carta, and collaboration with Zero Hash as reflecting its commitment to innovation and to introduce and educate retail clients to the value of advice.
items.quote: Strategic initiatives such as our recent acquisition of EquityZen, expanded partnership with Carta, and collaboration with Zero Hash all reflect our commitment to innovation... Our intentional strategy to introduce and educate retail clients to the value of advice

items.text: Morgan Stanley describes the early days of its digital asset transformation in wealth, including a partnership with Zero Hash, expansion into crypto and tokenized asset space, and continued work in E*TRADE for its active self-directed community.
items.quote: I would also call out just the early days of the digital asset transformation side of wealth. We announced a partnership with Zero Hash last year... We're well positioned now in the crypto and tokenized asset space... There is continued work that we're doing in E*TRADE

items.text: Morgan Stanley states its ability to serve clients across the private to public continuum continues to attract assets to its platform, delivering unique products, solutions, and advice, with growth led by workplace relationships from large IPOs of late-stage private workplace clients.
items.quote: Our ability to serve clients across the private to public continuum continues to attract assets to our world- class platform, delivering unique products, solutions, and advice.

a5.MS.reason: The passages describe specific products, services and platforms Morgan Stanley offers to attract and serve next-generation (founder/employee/early-stage) clients, so these are facts.

a6.MS.label: fact

items.text: Morgan Stanley's integrated firm capabilities chart lists 'Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning' among the offerings under the 'Preserve Wealth' stage of serving clients throughout their growth cycles.
items.quote: Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning

items.text: Morgan Stanley's CEO states that as a Morgan Stanley client you have access to ultra-high net worth family office infrastructure solutions.
items.quote: importantly, for ultra-high net worth family office infrastructure solutions

items.text: Morgan Stanley's CFO states the firm has done a lot of work on trying to service founders and family offices as part of growing its Wealth Management business.
items.quote: We've done a lot of work on trying to service founders, on trying to service family offices.

items.text: Morgan Stanley's CEO lists 'family office and OCIO' among the capabilities the firm is investing in for financial advisors that are difficult for others to replicate.
items.quote: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending

a6.MS.reason: The deck and transcripts describe family office solutions, trust and estate planning, and servicing family offices, which directly bear on engaging families and multi-generational wealth planning.

a7.MS.label: fact

items.text: Chairman and CEO Ted Pick said Morgan Stanley is focused on both public and private ecosystems, and that the objective is to cover growth companies and their employees from founding to their public maturity while broadening investor access to private companies.
items.quote: We are focused on both the public and the private ecosystems, augmented by our recent acquisition of EquityZen. The objective is to cover growth companies and their employees from founding to their public maturity while broadening access for investors to the growing stack of private companies.

items.text: Morgan Stanley's strategic update deck lays out an integrated-firm capability map spanning Corporates, Founders/Employees, Early Stage, and Public Company, including 'Founders Wealth Strategies,' 'Preserve Wealth,' and 'Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning.'
items.quote: Corporates / Founders / Employees / Early Stage / Public Company ... Financial Wellness and Employee Benefits ... Founders Wealth Strategies ... Preserve Wealth ... Full-Service Wealth Advice and Asset Allocation ... Family Office Solutions, Trust & Estate Planning

items.text: Ted Pick said the Morgan Stanley at Work business, with its exclusive partnership with Carta, positions the firm as an early trusted advisor to over 50,000 private companies, and that employees across workplace companies benefit from management of equity compensation plans, liquidity opportunities, and full-service advice.
items.quote: Our Morgan Stanley at Work business, with its exclusive partnership with Carta, positions us as an early trusted advisor to over 50,000 private companies.

items.text: CFO Sharon Yeshaya said Morgan Stanley has an exclusive partnership with Carta under which Carta will refer private stock-plan companies to Morgan Stanley as they move toward going public, creating a seamless experience for those clients.
items.quote: we have an exclusive partnership with Carta, which means that they will refer those private different stock plans or different corporate companies to Morgan Stanley as they move into going public.

items.text: CFO Sharon Yeshaya described how Morgan Stanley understands the full cap table and early investors, so that IPO-related flows (e.g., an endowment receiving stock) can move from a transfer agent into a Morgan Stanley advice-based relationship across different portions of the cap table.
items.quote: we have a full cap table. We understand early investors. And you can think, for example, of an endowment that might receive a stock associated with an IPO. He or she might take that and put it through from a transfer agent into a Morgan Stanley advice-based relationship.

items.text: Ted Pick said Morgan Stanley is using its scale to invest in broadening financial advisor capabilities including family office and OCIO, tailored lending, alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, and digitized assets.
items.quote: We are using our scale to invest in broadening capabilities for FAs that are difficult for others to replicate: alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets, family office and OCIO, and tailored lending.

a7.MS.reason: Passages contain leadership statements and strategic initiatives (integrated firm covering founders/employees through public maturity, Carta partnership, EquityZen, family office/trust and estate planning, IPO cap-table capture) that indicate commitment to capturing wealth transfer.

caveats: Net new assets as each firm defines it: Morgan Stanley: 'NNA represent client asset inflows, including interest, dividends and asset acquisitions, less client asset outflows, and excluding the impact of business...' (MS-10K-2025#166) | The Charles Schwab Corporation: defines a related metric instead: 'Core net new client assets: Net new client assets before significant one-time inflows or outflows, such as acquisitions/divestitures or extraordinary flows...' (SCHW-10K-2025#119) | Edward Jones: 'Net new assets represents cash and securities inflows and outflows, including fees and commissions and excluding mutual fund capital gain distributions...' (EDJ-10Q-2026Q2#60) | Merrill (Bank of America Corporation): defines a related metric instead: 'The net client AUM flows represent the net change in clients’ AUM balances over a specified period of time, excluding market appreciation/depreciation and...' (BAC-10K-2025#249) | Raymond James Financial: 'Domestic PCG net new assets represents domestic PCG client inflows, including dividends and interest, less domestic PCG client outflows, including commissions,...' (RJF-10K-2025#224).

Advisor headcount as each firm defines it: Morgan Stanley: 'Wealth Management representatives 15,950 15,469 15,468' (MS-SUPP-2020Q4#1); business lines in the count: 'Wealth Management representatives' (MS-SUPP-2020Q4#1); not stated: independent contractor advisors, trainees | The Charles Schwab Corporation: publishes no count of this metric; reports a related figure instead: 'perform investment advisory functions (including research)? 4127' (SCHW-ADV1A-2026#1); not stated: trainees | Edward Jones: 'Financial advisors (actual): At year end 20,425 20,125 19,232 1% Average 20,331 19,650 18,945 3%' (EDJ-10K-2025#130); independent contractor advisors: 'The Partnership’s financial advisors are employees or partners of the Partnership.' (EDJ-10K-2025#35); business lines in the count: 'two operating and reportable segments based upon geographic location, the U.S. and Canada' (EDJ-10K-2025#145); not stated: trainees | Merrill (Bank of America Corporation): '(3) Includes advisors across all wealth management businesses in GWIM and Consumer Banking.' (BAC-SUPP-2023Q4#2); business lines in the count: 'all wealth management businesses in GWIM and Consumer Banking' (BAC-SUPP-2023Q4#2); not stated: independent contractor advisors, trainees | Raymond James Financial: 'Advisors in our RCS division are not included in our financial advisor metric although their client assets are included in PCG AUA.' (RJF-10K-2025#228); independent contractor advisors: 'Independent contractors 5,065' (RJF-10K-2025#227); excludes: 'Advisors in our RCS division are not included' (RJF-10K-2025#228); not stated: trainees.

claims.text: Industry research: Cerulli (published October 29, 2025) projects that households will transfer $123.7 trillion to heirs ($105 trillion) and charities ($18 trillion) between now and 2048.
Industry research: Cerulli (published October 29, 2025) estimates that Generation Xers will inherit $39 trillion.
Industry research: Cerulli (published October 29, 2025) estimates that Millennials will inherit $46 trillion.

Industry research: UBS (published April 22, 2026) estimates that USD 83 trillion in private wealth will change hands globally over the next two to three decades (elsewhere described as the next two decades).
claims.source_label: Research research 2026-04-22, p.3 [research]; Research research 2026-04-22, p.6 [research]

claims.text: Industry research: Cerulli (published October 29, 2025) estimates that a total of $85 trillion of wealth owned by older generations will be donated or passed down to Gen X or Millennial heirs.

Schwab: In its 3Q25 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab states that while client assets are more concentrated among older generations today, the average age of its clients continues to get younger.
Schwab: As of September 30, 2026, Schwab states that approximately 70% of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Z and Millennials.
Schwab: As of September 30, 2026, Schwab states that approximately 75% of assets are retained in a wealth transfer event.

Schwab: In its 3Q25 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab states that industry research shows Gen Z is 45% more likely to start investing by the age of 21 as compared to Millennials.

Schwab: In its 3Q25 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab states that nearly one-third of new-to-firm retail households are Gen Zers, defined as investors between the ages of 13 and 28.
Schwab: In its 4Q24 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2024), Schwab states that 33% of its new-to-firm retail households are under the age of 30, and more than 50% are under the age of 40.

Schwab: In its 2Q25 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2025), Schwab states that one in six new-to-firm retail households are under age 24, more than 30% are under age 30, and nearly 60% are under age 40.

Schwab: In its 4Q25 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2025), Schwab states that Gen Z investors account for a large share of new retail client accounts opened in 2025, with the majority of those new accounts held by investors under age 40.
Schwab: In its 2Q26 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2026), Schwab states that 61% of affluent clients ages 25 to 44 prefer to consolidate their wealth and banking relationships.

Schwab: As of September 30, 2026, Schwab describes its client base as spanning generations from next-gen to retirees, wealth tiers from new investors to ultra high net worth, and investing styles from self-directed to advised.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones identifies the generational wealth transfer and changing client demographics, preferences and values among the strategic risks it seeks to address in light of the evolving financial services industry (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025).

Edward Jones: Edward Jones states that its continued ability to compete and adapt its business model may be adversely impacted by the generational wealth transfer, including changing client expectations for expanded product offerings and technology needs, and changing client demographics, preferences and values (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025).

Edward Jones: In its 2Q25 10-Q (period ended June 27, 2025), Edward Jones attributes higher asset outflows to a variety of factors including an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm, along with macroeconomic volatility, inflation and consumer spending.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones attributes the net new asset decrease in the first half of 2025 to factors including an aging client base and generational wealth transfers outside the firm, along with macroeconomic volatility, inflation and consumer spending (10-Q, period ended June 27, 2025).

Edward Jones: Edward Jones attributes the net new asset decline in the first nine months of 2025 to factors including an aging client base, generational wealth transfers outside the firm, macroeconomic volatility, inflationary pressures, and shifts in consumer spending (10-Q, period ended September 26, 2025).
Industry research: Cerulli (published October 29, 2025) states that wealth is more likely to be held by older households, a dynamic that has driven wealth transfer projections higher.

Industry research: Cerulli (published October 29, 2025) states that women in the Baby Boomer and older generations are expected to receive $40 trillion in 'horizontal' transfers as they outlive their husbands.
Industry research: Cerulli (published October 29, 2025) states that women in younger generations are expected to receive $47 trillion of the wealth to be transferred intergenerationally.
Industry research: UBS (published April 22, 2026) states that the Great Wealth Transfer is driven by aging demographics, longer life expectancies and decades of rising asset prices.

Industry research: UBS (published April 22, 2026) states that for the inheriting next generation, the process typically begins before formal inheritance, through participation in family discussions, governance structures, or growing responsibilities in a family business.

Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley's strategic update deck (published January 15, 2026) describes an integrated-firm client journey that includes Founders Wealth Strategies and, under Preserve Wealth, full-service wealth advice and asset allocation and family office solutions, trust and estate planning, indicating the firm retains wealth across generations through family office, trust and estate planning services.

Morgan Stanley: In its 4Q25 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2025), Morgan Stanley states it is investing to broaden capabilities for its financial advisors that include family office and OCIO, alongside alternatives and privates, tax-efficient investing, digitized assets and tailored lending, which support retaining multi-generational wealth.

Schwab: In its 4Q25 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2025), Schwab states it took an ownership stake in Wealth.com and began rolling out its estate analysis capability to specialists, giving the firm more tools to help clients integrate estate planning into their investment life.

Schwab: In its 2Q25 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2025), Schwab states it is enhancing its tax, trust, and estate capabilities, including plans to offer Wealth.com's estate planning tools to its retail clients.

Schwab: In its 1Q25 earnings call (period ended March 31, 2025), Schwab announced a strategic investment in Wealth.com, a leader in digital estate planning, to enhance its estate planning capabilities and experience for clients and its RIA ecosystem.

Schwab: In its 1Q26 earnings call (period ended March 31, 2026), Schwab states it launched the Schwab Teen Investor account for young people ages 13 to 17, giving them a way to start their investing journey and positioning the firm for next-generation relationships.

Schwab: In its 4Q25 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2025), Schwab states it is winning the young investor, with its average client age having fallen by about 10 years in the last decade and a third of its new-to-firm clients last year being Gen Z investors.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025) states that its continued ability to compete and adapt its business model may be adversely impacted by the evolving financial services industry and generational wealth transfer, including changing client expectations, demographics, preferences and values.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025) offers eligible retiring financial advisors individually tailored retirement transition plans that compensate them for providing client transition services, thereby transitioning client relationships to successor advisors.
Merrill: Merrill states it ranks No. 1 on Forbes' Top Next Generation Advisors (2025) and No. 1 on Financial Planning's Top 40 Advisors Under 40 List (2025).
Merrill: Merrill had 446 advisors named to the 2025 Forbes 'Top Next-Generation Wealth Advisors Best-in-State' list, more than any other firm (recruiting page content as of November 3, 2026).
claims.source_label: MER press page content as of 2026-11-03 [IR]

claims.text: Raymond James: Raymond James offers estate and charitable planning capabilities, lending and cash management solutions, risk management services, and intergenerational wealth strategies as tools its advisors can draw on when serving households with complex financial profiles, including affluent households (trade press, September 29, 2026).
Raymond James: Raymond James (10-K, fiscal year ended September 30, 2025) states that, generally, with planned retirements, assets are retained at the firm pursuant to advisor succession plans.

Raymond James: Raymond James (10-K, fiscal year ended September 30, 2025) states that it seeks to mitigate the risk of retiring advisors selling their practices to unaffiliated third parties through financial advisor succession planning and by providing financial advisors with a broad range of services and resources to support their practices.
Raymond James: Raymond James offers succession planning and acquisition support to independent RIAs as a way to plan for their next step (web page content as of July 12, 2026).
claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-07-12 [IR]

claims.text: Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management had 15,950 Wealth Management representatives (financial advisors) as of December 31, 2020.
Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management had 15,469 Wealth Management representatives as of September 30, 2020.
Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley's Wealth Management had 15,468 Wealth Management representatives as of December 31, 2019.

Morgan Stanley: Trade press (InvestmentNews, October 26, 2026) reports that Morgan Stanley for years has taken a small amount of an advisor's gross revenue, called it deferred compensation, and required advisors to stay for years in order to vest, a retention mechanism known as golden handcuffs.

Morgan Stanley: Trade press (InvestmentNews, October 26, 2026) reports that Morgan Stanley is not introducing retention bonuses as part of its 2027 pay plan for advisors, but is increasing a pay threshold for advisors by 10% in 2027, meaning advisors must generate that much more revenue to receive the same pay.

Morgan Stanley: In its 4Q25 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2025), Morgan Stanley states it will increase the cash component of its advisor compensation as it transitions deferred compensation plan economic hedges to derivative instruments, changes it says support its overall investment into its financial advisors and simplify its compensation program.

Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025) states its ability to retain and attract qualified employees is critical to its success, and that failure to attract, integrate, and retain highly qualified employees or successfully transition key roles may materially adversely affect its performance.

Morgan Stanley: In its 2Q25 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2025), Morgan Stanley notes advisor-led flows were particularly strong, originating from new advisors attracted to the strength of the workplace channel.

Schwab: Schwab (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025) maintains a financial consultant career achievement plan, a noncontributory, unfunded, nonqualified plan under which eligible financial consultants receive earned cash payments after retirement, contingent on meeting performance levels, tenure, age, and client transitioning requirements; full vesting occurs at age 60 with at least ten years of service.
Schwab: Schwab reported the projected benefit obligation of the financial consultant career achievement plan at $163 million at the end of 2025.
Schwab: Schwab reported the projected benefit obligation of the financial consultant career achievement plan at $134 million at the end of 2024.

Schwab: Schwab's Advisor Services (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025) offers access to business start-up and transition consultants, technology engineers, and dedicated service teams to support advisors establishing their own independent practices and throughout their transition.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025) states that eligible retiring financial advisors are offered individually tailored retirement transition plans that compensate a retiring financial advisor for successfully providing client transition services under a retirement and transition agreement, generally for five years.
Edward Jones: Edward Jones lists as a strategic priority to be the best firm to start, grow, optimize and pass on a practice (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025).

Edward Jones: In the second quarter of 2025 (10-Q, period ended June 27, 2025), Edward Jones' financial advisor attrition increased to 6.4% primarily due to an increase in retirements, consistent with industry trends.
Edward Jones: Edward Jones ended the second quarter of 2025 with 20,309 financial advisors.
Edward Jones: Edward Jones had 20,425 financial advisors at year end 2025.
Edward Jones: Edward Jones had 20,125 financial advisors at year end 2024.
Edward Jones: Edward Jones had 19,232 financial advisors at year end 2023.

Merrill: Merrill runs an Advisor Development Program to train new financial advisors, with roles designed to help participants identify client financial goals, align banking and investing solutions, and build a book of high-net-worth clients (recruiting page content as of November 3, 2026).
claims.source_label: MER press page content as of 2026-11-03 [IR]

claims.text: Merrill: Merrill's Advisor Development Program participants progress through three roles (Client Associate, Financial Solutions Advisor, and Financial Advisor) before graduating to Merrill Core Advisor, with the Financial Advisor role lasting approximately 1-4 years (recruiting page content as of November 3, 2026).
claims.source_label: MER press page content as of 2026-11-03 [IR]

claims.text: Merrill: In the 4Q25 earnings call (period ended December 31, 2025), Bank of America's CFO states Merrill is recruiting experienced advisors, but its primary strategy is a training program that trains people in wealth management at Bank of America and Merrill, which management believes drives improved net new flows.
Merrill: In the 2Q26 earnings call (period ended June 30, 2026), Merrill's management states it aims to keep growing the sales force, and advisor attrition is now at near historic lows.

Merrill: In the 1Q26 earnings call (period ended March 31, 2026), Merrill states it continues to attract talent across both new and experienced advisers, driving productivity higher on both newer and existing members of its financial advisers team.
Merrill: Merrill (across GWIM and Consumer Banking wealth management businesses) had 18,916 total wealth advisors at the end of 2023, down from 19,273 at the end of 2022.
Merrill: Merrill and the Private Bank have more than 15,000 wealth advisors (investor day deck, November 2025).

Merrill: The Forbes 'Top Next-Gen Wealth Advisors Best-in-State' list considers advisors born in 1986 or later with a minimum of four years as an advisor, indicating recognition of the firm's next-generation advisor pipeline.
claims.source_label: MER press page content as of 2026-11-03 [IR]

claims.source_label: RJF press page content as of 2026-05-19 [IR]

claims.text: Raymond James: Raymond James offers succession planning and acquisition resources plus a team of specialists to guide independent RIAs for their next step (web page content as of July 12, 2026).

claims.text: Raymond James: Raymond James has a 'next gen advisor strategy' as part of its collaborative recruiting across channels (investor day deck, June 2025).

Morgan Stanley: Morgan Stanley's strategic update deck (published January 15, 2026) shows the firm serves founders and employees across their growth cycle (from early stage through public company) with offerings including Founders Wealth Strategies, private shares trading and lending, IPO execution and support services, financial wellness and employee benefits, full-service wealth advice and asset allocation, family office solutions, trust and estate planning, and unlocking liquidity.

Morgan Stanley: In 3Q25 (period ended September 30, 2025), Morgan Stanley reports it continues to invest to deepen competitive moats, including an expanded collaboration with Carta in private markets and in digital assets through announced partnerships with Zero Hash.

Morgan Stanley: In 2025, Morgan Stanley identifies strategic initiatives such as its acquisition of EquityZen, expanded partnership with Carta, and collaboration with Zero Hash as reflecting its commitment to innovation and to introduce and educate retail clients to the value of advice.

Morgan Stanley: In 2025, Morgan Stanley describes the early days of its digital asset transformation in wealth, including a partnership with Zero Hash, expansion into crypto and tokenized asset space, and continued work in E*TRADE for its active self-directed community.

Morgan Stanley: In 2Q26 (period ended June 30, 2026), Morgan Stanley states its ability to serve clients across the private to public continuum continues to attract assets to its platform, delivering unique products, solutions, and advice, with growth led by workplace relationships from large IPOs of late-stage private workplace clients.
Schwab: Schwab lists Schwab Starter Kit and Schwab Teen Investor Account as offerings for younger investors, alongside no/low commissions (investor day deck, May 2026).

Schwab: Schwab (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025) supports newer investors with accessible products such as Schwab Stock Slices and the Schwab Starter Kit, along with trading capabilities, advisory solutions, and educational resources.

Schwab: Schwab (10-Q, period ended June 30, 2026) began a phased rollout to retail clients of Schwab Crypto, its spot crypto trading offer providing direct access to bitcoin and ether trading combined with educational content and professional support.

Schwab: In its 3Q25 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab's CEO stated crypto will certainly appeal to young investors and will help attract the next generation, while noting Schwab is already winning with young investors today.

Schwab: In its 3Q25 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab's CEO said the support, service, education, and leading thinkorswim platform and digital capabilities offered to young investors is unmatched, which is why Schwab is succeeding with young investors.

Schwab: In its 3Q25 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab's CEO said younger investors' top online resource is YouTube, and Schwab is the number one financial services firm on YouTube by followers; Schwab meets younger clients in the channels where they turn for information.

Schwab: In its 3Q25 earnings call (period ended September 30, 2025), Schwab states it puts on 35 hours a week of live content teaching investors how to trade and invest, and has about a thousand former trading professionals answering phones for investors seeking advice and expertise.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025) states it is pursuing a new digital platform focused on attracting and retaining Next Generation investors, as one of its recently launched or in-development initiatives.

Edward Jones: Trade press reports (August 18, 2026) that Edward Jones has taken a minority stake in the personal finance app Quicken, intending to integrate Quicken's personal financial management capabilities more directly into Edward Jones to support its value proposition and advisor conversations with clients.

Edward Jones: Edward Jones (10-K, fiscal year ended December 31, 2025) states it has been making investments in initiatives to meet clients' comprehensive needs, including Financial Planning Services (a more personalized experience with additional planning capabilities), High Net Worth (expanded advice and planning across multiple service models), and Workplace (connecting local business owners and their employees with financial solutions).

Raymond James: Raymond James' private wealth infrastructure includes intergenerational wealth strategies, positioned as a tool advisors can draw on when serving households with complex financial profiles (trade press, September 29, 2026).

The client assets per advisor figures cannot be validly compared side by side across the five firms. The client asset measures differ in definition: Morgan Stanley's client assets is the sum of Wealth Management client assets and Investment Management AUM, with its advisor-led channel (client assets in accounts with a Wealth Management representative assigned) of $5,715 billion at December 31, 2025 excluding self-directed and workplace channels; Schwab's total client assets span brokerage accounts, workplace plan participant accounts, banking accounts, and custodial assets held for independent advisors; Edward Jones uses client assets under care (AUC); Merrill uses client balances composed of assets under management, brokerage and other assets, deposits, and loans and leases; and Raymond James uses client assets under administration (AUA), itself cautioning that 'The definitions for client assets may be inconsistent across companies.' The advisor counts also differ in definition: Morgan Stanley reports Wealth Management representatives (15,950 at December 31, 2020); Schwab reports no financial-advisor headcount (only approximately 4,127 employees performing investment advisory functions, more than 16,000 independent RIA firms, or approximately 33,000 full-time employees); Edward Jones reports financial advisors (actual), distinct from a full-time equivalent basis; Merrill's available count spans all wealth management businesses in GWIM and Consumer Banking (or Merrill plus Private Bank), not Merrill alone; and Raymond James counts employee and independent contractor advisors while excluding RCS-division advisors whose assets are nonetheless included in AUA. Because the numerators, denominators, and their definitions all differ, and because the per-advisor figures are stand-in components rather than a shared disclosed metric, the figures are not on the same basis and cannot be validly compared.
